oneIdea: Many integrals have no neat formula, so we cut the area into thin strips and add up simple shapes (rectangles, trapezoids, parabolas). A differential equation only tells you the slope at each point, so we use the same add-up-small-pieces idea: start at the known point, step along the slope, repeat. Smarter shapes or smarter steps give more accuracy for the same work.
goals: Explain a definite integral as an area and say why we approximate it by strips of width \(\Delta x=(b-a)/n\).
Apply the midpoint, trapezoidal and Simpson 1/3 rules by hand, including the weights \(1,2,\dots,2,1\) and \(1,4,2,\dots,4,1\).
Say why Simpson's 1/3 rule needs an even \(n\) and why \(1,4,4,1\) is wrong.
Explain the idea of Gaussian quadrature (choose the points) and adaptive quadrature (split only where the function is hard).
Read \(dy/dx=f(x,y)\) as a slope rule and take Euler steps \(y_{i+1}=y_i+h\,f(x_i,y_i)\) by hand.
Say why Runge-Kutta is more accurate than Euler and use MATLAB's ode45 and integral.

intro.idea: An integral is an area under a curve. Numerical integration cuts \([a,b]\) into \(n\) equal strips of width \(\Delta x=(b-a)/n\) and adds up the areas of simple shapes.
intro.mistake: Using \(\Delta x=(b-a)/(n+1)\) or forgetting to multiply by \(\Delta x\) at the end. With \(n\) strips the width is \((b-a)/n\), and every rule needs that factor.

check.q: You integrate over \([0,6]\) with \(n=3\) strips. What is \(\Delta x\)?

mid.idea: Replace each strip by a rectangle whose height is \(f\) at the middle of the strip. Then add the heights and multiply by \(\Delta x\).
mid.mistake: Evaluating \(f\) at the strip edges instead of the midpoints. The midpoints of \([0,10]\) with \(n=5\) are \(1,3,5,7,9\), not \(0,2,4,\dots\).

check.q: Midpoint rule for \(\int_0^4 x^2\,dx\) with \(n=2\). What is the estimate?
check.why: \(\Delta x=2\), midpoints \(1\) and \(3\): \(2(1^2+3^2)=2(10)=20\). The exact value is \(64/3\approx21.3\).

trap.idea: Join neighbouring points with straight lines and add the trapezoids. The end values count once, every interior value counts twice, because two trapezoids share it: weights \(1,2,2,\dots,2,1\), times \(\Delta x/2\).
trap.mistake: Giving the end points weight 2 as well, or forgetting the factor \(\Delta x/2\) (half, not full \(\Delta x\)).

check.q: Trapezoidal rule for \(\int_0^2 x^2\,dx\) with \(n=2\) (points \(0,1,2\)). What is the estimate?
check.why: \(\Delta x=1\): \(\tfrac12[0+2(1)+4]=3\). It overshoots the exact \(8/3\) because the curve bends upward, so the chords lie above it.

simp.idea: Fit a parabola through every pair of strips. The weights follow the pattern \(1,4,2,4,\dots,2,4,1\), times \(\Delta x/3\). It is exact for cubics.
simp.mistake: Using Simpson's 1/3 rule with an odd number of segments (for example 4 points, \(n=3\)) and writing \(1,4,4,1\). Strips must pair up, so \(n\) must be even; the weights must add up to \(3n\).

check.q: Which weight list is correct for Simpson's 1/3 rule with \(n=6\)?
check.why: Odd-index points get 4, even interior points get 2, ends get 1. Check: the sum is \(18=3n\).

quad.idea: Gaussian quadrature chooses where to sample: \(n\) well-placed points are exact for polynomials up to degree \(2n-1\). Adaptive quadrature chooses where to use more strips: it compares one parabola with two on each strip and splits only where they disagree.
quad.mistake: Applying the table of nodes for \([-1,1]\) directly to another interval. You must first map the nodes with \(x=\tfrac{b-a}{2}t+\tfrac{a+b}{2}\) and multiply by \(\tfrac{b-a}{2}\).

check.q: 2-point Gauss on \([-1,1]\) uses nodes \(\pm1/\sqrt3\) with weights 1, 1. For \(\int_{-1}^{1}t^2\,dt\) it gives
check.why: \(1\cdot\tfrac13+1\cdot\tfrac13=\tfrac23\), which is exact, because 2 points are exact up to degree \(2(2)-1=3\).

ode.idea: In \(dy/dx=f(x,y)\), the function \(f\) is a slope rule: give it a point and it returns the slope of the solution there. The initial value \(y(x_0)=y_0\) picks one curve from the family.
ode.mistake: Treating \(f(x,y)\) as the solution itself. It is the slope, not the height \(y\).

check.q: For \(dy/dx=x+y\), what is the slope of the solution at the point \((1,2)\)?

euler.idea: Euler's method: new height = old height + step width \(\times\) slope at the current point, \(y_{i+1}=y_i+h\,f(x_i,y_i)\). Repeat until you reach the \(x\) you want. It is first order: halving \(h\) roughly halves the error.
euler.mistake: Using the slope at the end of the step, or forgetting to multiply by \(h\). Euler uses the slope at the start and moves by \(h\cdot\)slope.

check.q: \(dy/dx=2y\), \(y(0)=1\), \(h=0.1\). What is \(y_1\) from one Euler step?

rk.idea: Runge-Kutta samples the slope several times across each step and averages them. RK4 uses weights \(1,2,2,1\) and is fourth order, so it can take much larger steps than Euler. ode45 also adapts the step size automatically.
rk.mistake: Thinking more slope samples are just extra work. Each RK4 step costs 4 evaluations of \(f\), but the error shrinks so fast that it still wins by a wide margin.

check.q: You halve the step size \(h\) in RK4 (fourth order). The error drops by about
check.why: Fourth order means error \(\propto h^4\), and \(2^4=16\). For Euler (first order) halving \(h\) only halves the error.
